# Identification of actionable tweets during Philippine disasters using machine learning

Alyanna T. Somido<sup>\*</sup>and Reinabelle C. Reyes

National Institute of Physics, University of the Philippines Diliman, Quezon City, Philippines 1101 Corresponding author: asomido@nip.up.edu.ph

## Abstract

Successful disaster response requires time-critical information, of which one abundant source is social media such as Twitter. However, because of the sheer volume of tweets, as well as their short, unstructured nature, it is challenging and time-consuming to find tweets that contain actionable information. In this study, we developed logistic regression binary classification models to classify tweets on whether they provide information about the on-the-ground situation during a disaster, i.e., their informativeness. We trained and tested our models using tweets from the CrisisLexT26 dataset concerning five disasters which occurred in the Philippines during 2012 to 2013. We compared models using different feature sets extracted using the Bag-of-Words (BoW), and TF-IDF vectorization methods, in conjunction with word embedding using word2vec, and evaluated their accuracy, precision, recall, AUC, and F1-scores. Our results indicate that relatively simple models using BoW and TF-IDF features are able to achieve good performance, comparable to that of more sophisticated models made for similar applications. We attribute this to the difference in scope, which points to the potential of a country-specific training approach. This is supported by our identification of the most important keywords in predicting the informativeness of a tweet. We found that words and hashtags related to calls for donation, impacts of disasters, and specific events are most associated with informative tweets while those associated with sympathy, such as ‘pray’, and ‘#prayforvisayas’, were most associated with non-informative tweets. These models show promise in automating the identification of useful and relevant tweets to support disaster response efforts.

Keywords: natural language processing, machine learning, social media, disasters

## 1 Introduction

Successful disaster response requires time-critical information, of which one abundant source is social media such as Twitter. Their accessibility means that it is relatively easy for those in affected areas to share firsthand information of the event, which would be otherwise difficult to obtain [1]. Such information can be vital to quick and effective disaster response. This is particularly of interest for the Philippines, a country characterized by frequent disasters such as typhoons, flooding and earthquakes. It also boasts one of the fastest growing populations of social media users [2]. However, because of the sheer volume of tweets, their short, unstructured nature, their usage of slang, and in some cases their mixed use of languages, it can be difficult and time-consuming to identify the informative tweets from the non-informative ones.

In this study, we use the Twitter data for five Philippine disaster events from the CrisisLexT26 dataset [3] to train machine learning models to identify informative tweets. Each model is developed using a different combination of commonly used natural language processing techniques for feature extraction, namely Bag-of-Words (BoW), TF-IDF, and word2vec. We then evaluate and compare the performance of these models with each other as well as with similar models in the literature.

## 2 Methodology

## 2.1 Data Collection and Pre-processing

We used the publicly available dataset CrisisLexT26<sup>1</sup>, which consists of tweet text collected from 26 different disaster events which occurred from 2012 to 2013. Of these 26 events, we chose the five which occurred in the Philippines whose details are listed in Table 1. This subset contains a total of 5000 tweets, labeled for informativeness. These were labelled by crowdsourced workers based on the definition given by Olteanu et. al. [3] that an informative tweet must contain helpful information which helped one understand the situation during the ongoing disaster event.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>1</sup>[https://crisislex.org/data-collections.html#CrisisLexT26](https://crisislex.org/data-collections.html#CrisisLexT26)</span></small>

We split the data in an 80 to 20 train-test split, ensuring that there were an equal number of tweets from each event in both the train and test sets.

Table 1: List of disaster events included in the dataset used in this study

| Disaster Event | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Philippine Floods | Floods in August 2012 caused by the South-west Monsoon or Hanging Habagat |
| Typhoon Pablo | Typhoon in November 2012 known interna-tionally as Typhoon Bopha |
| Bohol Earthquake | 7.2 magnitude earthquake which occurred on Oct. 15, 2013 in Bohol |
| Manila Floods | Floods in August 2013 caused by both the Southwest Monsoon and Typhoon Maring |
| Typhoon Yolanda | Typhoon during November 2013 known inter-nationally as Typhoon Haiyan |

For pre-processing, we used the built-in TweetTokenizer from the NLTK python library, setting the parameters reduce len and strip handle to True. This sets the tokenizer to reduce the length of long strings of the same character to 3, and to strip user handles from the text.

The target variable for our models was ‘informativeness’ as labelled in the CrisisLexT26 dataset, which was manually annotated by crowd-sourced workers. An informative tweet was defined to be one containing useful information that helps the reader understand the situation in the ongoing crisis event.

## 2.2 Model Development

We developed logistic regression models that classify tweets as either informative or non-informative. We chose logistic regression over other binary classification models that have been used for this task (e.g., LibLinear [4], Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machines, Neural Networks [5], etc.) for its simplicity and easy implementation. In addition, the coefficients of logistic regression models can also be used directly as a measure of feature importance, which we could then make use of to gain further insights on our model.

We then tested how performance varied for 4 different feature sets, BoW and TF-IDF with and without word embedding using word2vec. The BoW and TF-IDF models features were extracted using the NLTK library’s [6] CountVectorizer and TfIdfVectorizer with the default settings. For the word2vec features, we used the gensim library’s [7] implementation of a pre-trained GloVe Twitter 200 word2vec model [8]. The word2vec + BoW and word2vec + TF-IDF features use these word-embeddings to create a document vector by taking the average of a tweet’s word vectors, using either the BoW or TF-IDF vectors as weights.

## 2.3 Model Selection and Evaluation

Our logistic Regression models return a probability that a tweet is informative. Here, we assign a threshold equal to the value that maximizes the geometric mean of the sensitivity, or True Positive Rate (TPR), and specificity, or the inverse of the False Positive Rate (1 - FPR):

$$
g = \sqrt {T P R \times (1 - F P R)}\tag{1}
$$

A tweet is classified as informative if the predicted probability is above this threshold. All models are compared in terms of commonly-used performance measures for binary classification models: accuracy, AUC, precision, recall and F-score.

## 3 Results

## 3.1 Model Performance

In Table 2, we compare the models’ performances in terms of accuracy, AUC, precision, recall, and Fscore. Examining these results, we find that the Bag-of-Words (BoW) model had the best performance in all measures except for recall, where the Word2vec + BoW model yielded the best performance.

Previous work, such as To et. al. (2017) [9] found that machine learning-based methods for identifying informative tweets suffer from lower recall, between 0.25 to 0.50, compared to keyword matching-based methods. In contrast, our results have demonstrated that a simple BoW model for identifying informative tweets performs well in both precision and recall, reaching 0.95 and 0.86 for each metric respectively. These learning-based models have the advantage that they do not require human-made keyword or hashtag lists in order to classify the tweets. The BoW and TF-IDF models also resulted in performance measures comparable to other models developed in previous work for similar applications [4, 5].

Table 2: Performance measures for all of the models, with the best score per measure in bold

| Feature Set | Accuracy | AUC | Precision | Recall | F-Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BoW | 0.8778 | 0.9394 | 0.9471 | 0.8550 | 0.8987 |
| TF-IDF | 0.8697 | 0.9359 | 0.9309 | 0.8583 | 0.8931 |
| Word2vec + BoW | 0.8677 | 0.9101 | 0.9041 | 0.8854 | 0.8946 |
| Word2vec + TF-IDF | 0.8556 | 0.9160 | 0.9103 | 0.8567 | 0.8827 |

One possible reason why, in this case, a simple, quickly-trained BoW model is able to achieve comparable or better performance compared to more sophisticated models in the literature is our application to a limited scope, in this case, training models specifically for Philippine disaster events rather than on a global dataset. This allowed the model to hone in on a particular set of keywords commonly used in this specific context, as we demonstrate in the next section.

## 3.2 Relevant Keywords from Feature Importance

For logistic regression models, the best-fit coefficients directly provide a measure of feature importance. Because the BoW and TF-IDF model features are directly related to specific words, we were able to investigate the words that each model identified as being most indicative of informative and non-informative tweets, by ranking words according to their corresponding coefficients.

Figures 1 and 2 show word cloud visualizations of the words most associated with informative and non-informative tweets (left and right panels, respectively) according to the BoW and TF-IDF models. The most important words for informative tweets include words associated with calls for donations (such as ‘donate’ and ‘donations’), hashtags related to the disaster event (such as ‘#typhoonhaiyan’ and ‘#reliefph’), and words related to the impact of the disaster (such as ‘hits’ and ‘dead’). The most important words for non-informative tweets are dominated by words and hashtags of sympathy and encouragement, such as ‘love’, ‘prayers’ and ‘#prayforvisayas’.

## 4 Conclusions

In this work, we developed machine learning models using commonly-used natural language processing techniques such as BoW, TF-IDF, and word2vec, and trained them on a publicly available dataset of tweets associated with five disaster events which occurred in the Philippines. Our results indicate relatively simple models using features from BoW and TF-IDF models are able to achieve similar performance results to more sophisticated models developed in previous work for similar applications. Though further investigation is needed to evaluate potential reasons for this result, we speculate that the difference in the models’ scopes can be a relevant factor— specifically, as a consequence of focusing our models to cover only disaster events in the Philippines (as opposed to a global or U.S. scope consisting of a larger variation of events, locations, and contexts), they were able to identify specific keywords and exploit them to correctly identify tweets as informative or not.

It will be interesting to test how these pre-trained models will perform for more recent disaster events in the Philippines, as well as whether this approach of training country-specific models will generalize to other countries as well. Further work in this direction can potentially significantly contribute towards the efficient automation of identification of useful and relevant tweets to support disaster response efforts.
